title: [CLO Beginner's Guide] Analog Control_Comprehensive Adjustment
description: CLO Beginner's Tutorial: By studying courses related to [Simulation Control], master more practical tools for garment adjustment, comprehensively apply them to improve simulation stability and optimize garment shape. Gradually advance to mastering garment production techniques.

In this section, we are conducting a comprehensive practice.  
Open and adjust the leisure suit file.  
There are currently many simulation issues with this leisure suit.  
Let's focus on the solutions.  
Before performing specific operations, let's first reduce the quality of the clothing.  
Select one of the panels.  
You can see that the particle size of the panel is currently 5 mm.  
We can press Ctrl + A to select all panels.  
Change the particle size of the panels to 12 mm.  
To increase simulation speed, you can manually modify the particle size.  
You can also use the reduce quality tool to lower the quality.  
Long press the increase quality tool.  
You can switch to the reduce quality tool.  
The reduce quality tool will by default reduce the particle size of all panels.  
Use the reduce quality tool to reduce to 20 mm.  
Reduce the collision thickness to 2.5 mm.  
Change the model surface to 3 mm.  
The reduced specific values can also be manually adjusted.  
First, let's address the most obvious sleeve wear issue.  
On the left side, find the selection grid tool.  
First, locate the worn part of the frame selection arm in the 3D window.  
Find the target grid area that is blocked.  
Perform the frame selection.  
Press Ctrl + Shift to select.  
Press Ctrl to select.  
After selecting,  
in the 3D window,  
in the green grid area,  
press the left mouse button.  
Remove the positioning ball.  
Rotate to the right angle.  
Use the axis of the positioning ball.  
Push this part of the grid out.  
Let it wrap around the arm again.  
Then press the Control key to simulate.  
The worn part is repaired.  
Next,  
look at the bottom of the left front piece.  
This is a folding structure.  
Now the folding part inside should have come out.  
We also use the selection grid tool.  
Select the grid on the bottom right side.  
Push it slightly inward.  
Note that there are pants underneath.  
Do not push too much.  
Otherwise, the frame selection will reverse.  
It should be on the outer grid.  
Pull it out.  
The back side is also treated.  
The back side is also treated.  
The back side is also treated.  
The back side is also treated.  
The back side is also treated.  
After adjusting the volume and sleeve,  
you can see the hat below.  
The hat shakes obviously during simulation.  
This indicates there may be a wear issue here.  
You can check by selecting the panel.  
You will find the side part of the wear is outside.  
Then the glued edges of these three pieces are problematic.  
We can select all the glued edges from the 2D window and add them to the 3D version.  
Then, in simulation mode,  
pull the hat down with your small hand.  
Use the hand tool to hold the hat down.  
Use the hand tool to hold the hat down.  
If you pass the film again during the process, you can redo the operation of adding the right-click to the inside.  
There is a small panel at the entrance, which should normally be hooked to the other side, but currently it is not fixed.  
We can use the fake sewing tool to fix it directly to the corresponding panel with a point.  
If the position of the click in the 3D window is not accurate enough, you can use the editor’s fake sewing tool to adjust the point in the 2D window to make the simulation effect more natural.  
Then check again whether the clothes are correct, such as whether the gap between the collar and the side is even, and whether the shoulder lines are level on both sides.  
Now we find that the entire top is slightly tilted left and right.  
You can double-click to select it.  
In the front view, use the positioning ball circle to rotate the whole piece.  
After rotating, to avoid instability in simulation of the clothes and pants,  
select the top panel.  
On the right side, change the layer in the attribute editor from 0 to 1.  
The first time you do this, a pop-up will appear indicating that all non-zero layer panels will display light and light ratio for identification.  
You can set this without prompts.  
Just click Yes.  
By default, all panel layers are 0.  
Now the layer of the top 1 panel is set to 1, which is the outer layer of the pants.  
After modifying the layer, press the Control key to simulate.  
If it is still tilted left and right, you can double-click again to select the entire garment, rotate it, and simulate until the clothes are correct.  
Then press shortcut keys 4 or 6 to switch to the side view.  
You will find the whole garment is tilted backward.  
The front and back of the bottom are misaligned.  
Similarly, double-click to select the entire garment.  
In side view, use the positioning ball to rotate it forward.  
After rotating to a certain angle, start the simulation.  
You can rotate it again until the adjustment is correct.  
If you find that the button on the pants has come out, you can select the button and push it in.  
Or to prevent the button and pants from wearing, you can select the two front panels and push them out to cover the button.  
Then simulate.  
After adjusting the balance of the clothing, double-click again to select the whole garment and rotate the layer back to 0.  
In addition, for left and right parallel panels, you can align them.  
For example, the sleeves.  
Assuming the sleeves on the right side simulate better,  
you can directly select the parallel panel pattern on the left and copy the good pattern from the right side to the left.  
This technique is also applicable when initially adjusting the sleeves to deal with partial wear of symmetrical panels.  
Finally, for the top,  
since the fabric of this top has different colors on the front and back,  
for the hat side, we can select all the sides.  
In 3D, right-click to select the surface and rotate it.  
Switch the front and back of the fabric.  
Then select the top and bottom.  
Then select the top and bottom.  
Then select the top and bottom.  
After adjusting the top,  
double-click to select the pants, and click the selection tool on the left.  
This way, the view only shows the pants, making it easier to check problems.  
Because the pants color is darker,  
we can switch the clothing dye type to black-and-white surface,  
which makes it clearer and allows us to distinguish the front and back of the fabric.  
First, we find the sewing direction on the pants is reversed.  
We need to use the edit sewing line tool.  
Select the short purple sewing line above.  
Right-click to select change sewing line.  
Then switch back to the select and move tool.  
On the pants panel, right-click to add to the outside.  
Re-model.  
Next, look at the hem.  
Select the hem.  
You will find that the hem edge is outside.  
We can use the set layer tool.  
First select the outer pants.  
Then select the hem edge inside.  
After setting the layer,  
press the Control key to simulate,  
it will return to the inside.  
If there is still some wear or unevenness inside,  
you can select the pants,  
right-click to hide the 3D pattern.  
Press Shift + Q.  
You can use the hardening tool.  
During modeling,  
pull the small hem pattern straight.  
After adjustment,  
remove the hardening of the hem pattern.  
Then press Shift + W  
to display all patterns.  
So, the pants are also adjusted.  
After adjustment,  
the pants will be restored to a dense pattern surface display.  
Finally, click again to isolate the selection,  
display all clothes and models,  
and perform a general inspection.  
After confirming the adjustments,  
use the increase quality tool to raise the quality,  
and simulate again.  
The tools used in 2D switch back and forth.  
After completing the adjustments,  
use the increase quality tool to enhance quality,  
and simulate again.  
The 2D tools switch back and forth to adjust the patterns.  
Finally,  
under increased quality,  
you can optimize the adjustment details.  
Thus,  
the comprehensive adjustment of this leisure suit is complete.

chunks.content: ## Overview of Comprehensive Adjustment for Analog Control in CLO This section details a step-by-step procedure for adjusting a leisure suit garment in CLO using analog control techniques. It covers quality reduction, panel selection, grid manipulation, handling wear issues, layer adjustments, fabric orientation, sewing corrections, and final quality enhancements to optimize simulation and garment fit. --- ## Reducing Simulation Complexity by Adjusting Particle Size and Quality To speed up simulation and reduce computational load, start by lowering the garment’s particle size and overall quality settings: - Select any panel and observe that the initial particle size is 5 mm. - Press **Ctrl + A** to select all panels. - Increase particle size to 12 mm manually or use the **Reduce Quality Tool** to set particle size to 20 mm. - Adjust collision thickness to 2.5 mm and model surface thickness to 3 mm. - These values can be manually fine-tuned to balance between simulation speed and visual fidelity. --- ## Repairing Sleeve Wear and Frame Selection Adjustments Wear issues on the sleeves and frame parts cause simulation glitches. Use the **Selection Grid Tool** to identify and fix these: - Locate worn frame areas in the 3D window, particularly on the left sleeve. - Select the problematic grid area, remove the positioning ball, and rotate it to a proper angle. - Push the grid out so it properly wraps around the arm. - Simulate with **Ctrl** pressed to verify repair. For folds at the bottom of the left front piece: - Use the selection grid tool to push the inward grid slightly, taking care not to reverse the frame selection. - Pull out the outer grid carefully, considering underlying pants to avoid collision. --- ## Stabilizing Loose Components: Hat Wear and Fake Sewing Fixes Simulation instability, such as a shaking hat, often indicates wear or misalignment at glued edges: - Check panels adjacent to the hat to identify worn edges. - Select glued edges in the 2D window and add them to the 3D version. - Use the **Hand Tool** in simulation mode to hold and adjust the hat position. - Fix small unhooked panels at entrances using the **Fake Sewing Tool** by attaching points directly to corresponding panels. - Adjust fake sewing points in the 2D editor for precise simulation behavior. --- ## Correcting Garment Tilt and Layering for Stability Balancing the garment orientation is crucial for realistic simulation: - Identify tilt by checking collar gaps and shoulder line alignment. - Select the entire garment and rotate it using the positioning ball in the front view to correct left-right tilt. - Change the layer of the top panel from 0 to 1 in the attribute editor to position it as an outer layer relative to pants; confirm the prompt by clicking Yes. - After rotation, simulate to check stability and repeat corrections until balanced. - Use shortcut keys **4** or **6** to switch to side view for checking front-back tilt.

chunks.content: - Select the entire garment and rotate it using the positioning ball in the front view to correct left-right tilt. - Change the layer of the top panel from 0 to 1 in the attribute editor to position it as an outer layer relative to pants; confirm the prompt by clicking Yes. - After rotation, simulate to check stability and repeat corrections until balanced. - Use shortcut keys **4** or **6** to switch to side view for checking front-back tilt. - Rotate the garment forward or backward as necessary and simulate until properly aligned. --- ## Adjusting Buttons and Symmetrical Panels to Prevent Wear Buttons and symmetrical garment parts often require precise adjustments to avoid simulation errors: - If buttons on pants protrude, push them inward or push the front panels outward to cover buttons. - For symmetrical panels like sleeves, copy the better-simulated pattern from one side to the other to fix partial wear. - This method ensures uniformity and reduces repeated wear issues. --- ## Flipping Fabric Orientation and Color Differentiation For garments with different fabric colors on front and back: - Select all edges of the hat side panels in 3D. - Right-click to select the surface and rotate to flip front and back fabric sides. - This ensures correct fabric display and simulation behavior. --- ## Pants Adjustment: Sewing Direction and Hem Correction Pants often require detailed sewing and hem corrections: - Use the **Edit Sewing Line Tool** to select sewing lines with reversed direction (e.g., short purple lines). - Right-click to change sewing line direction. - Add pants panels to the outside using right-click and remodel. - Inspect the hem edge; if it is outside, use the **Set Layer Tool** to move the hem edge inside relative to the outer pants. - Simulate with **Ctrl** to confirm correction. - For persistent wear or unevenness inside the hem, hide 3D patterns with **Shift + Q** and apply the **Hardening Tool** to pull and straighten hem patterns. - Remove hardening after adjustment and display all patterns with **Shift + W**. --- ## Final Inspection and Quality Enhancement After all adjustments: - Isolate selections to inspect pants or other garment parts separately. - Switch pants clothing dye type to **Black-and-White Surface** to better distinguish fabric front and back. - Perform a general inspection of the entire garment and model. - Use the **Increase Quality Tool** to restore particle size and collision thickness to higher levels. - Simulate at increased quality to optimize fine adjustment details. - Use 2D tools to toggle and refine patterns during final simulation. - This completes the comprehensive adjustment of the leisure suit, ensuring stability, proper fit, and realistic cloth behavior. --- # Summary This guide covers practical techniques in CLO for analog control and comprehensive garment adjustment, including particle size management, grid and frame correction, sewing and layering adjustments, fabric orientation, and final quality optimization. Following these steps improves simulation speed, reduces wear, and enhances garment realism for complex clothing like leisure suits.
